metaData.originalTitle: 从零设计生产级 Multi-Agent Harness：架构、评估、记忆、成本与 MCP 工具接入全拆解
metaData.title: Designing a Production-Grade Multi-Agent Harness from Scratch: Architecture, Evaluation, Memory, Cost, and MCP Tool Integration
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically deconstructs the design principles and engineering practices of a production-grade Multi-Agent Harness, covering architecture orchestration, tool governance, state and memory, evaluation systems, cost control, and MCP integration.
metaData.summary: The article points out that most teams' Multi-Agent systems remain at the demo stage, and the real barrier to production deployment is not model capability but the lack of a reliable runtime foundation—a Multi-Agent Harness. The author defines the Harness as the "operating system" for agents and elaborates on five core modules: architecture orchestration emphasizes that "agents handle local intelligence, while the Harness handles global control," recommending declarative planning; tool governance proposes a Tool Registry as a unified gateway, requiring nine metadata fields for each tool; state and memory distinguish between State and Memory, highlighting the importance of a forgetting mechanism; the evaluation system suggests a four-layer approach (component, trajectory, task completion, and end-to-end), noting the limitations of LLM-as-Judge; cost control introduces Token Budget, model routing, context compression, and tiered degradation strategies. Finally, the article discusses the significance of the MCP protocol for standardizing the tool ecosystem and presents a three-phase roadmap from MVP to scale. The article is accompanied by multiple PlantUML diagrams, making it a high-value engineering practice guide.
metaData.featuredReason: Tencent Cloud's team makes the call directly: what determines whether multi-agent systems ship to production isn't the model or the prompt — it's the often-overlooked Harness, the agent's operating system. The production rule is one sentence: agents handle local intelligence, the harness handles global control. The orchestrator must own five decisions exclusively — task lifecycle, execution plan adjudication, agent routing, failure handling, and hard termination gates. Five core modules (orchestration, tool governance, memory, evaluation, cost control) each get a PlantUML diagram, with MCP tool integration covered separately. The most complete multi-agent engineering playbook to come out of China this year.

mainPoints.point: The core of a production-grade Multi-Agent system is the Harness, not a more powerful model or prompt.
mainPoints.explanation: The Harness is responsible for orchestration, scheduling, memory, state, tool governance, budget control, and observability. It acts as the "operating system" for agents, determining whether a system can move from demo to production.

mainPoints.point: Architecture orchestration should follow the principle that "agents handle local intelligence, while the Harness handles global control."
mainPoints.explanation: The Orchestrator must exclusively hold five decision rights: task lifecycle management, execution plan adjudication, agent routing, failure handling, and hard termination conditions. The Planner should output declarative plans rather than imperative calls.

mainPoints.point: Tools must be governed uniformly through a Tool Registry, rather than being called as ordinary functions.
mainPoints.explanation: Each tool must register nine metadata fields, including name, description, parameter schema, RBAC, timeout, risk level, and human-in-the-loop requirements, and must go through the unified gateway from day one.

mainPoints.point: The evaluation system should be layered, with a focus on execution trajectories rather than just the final answer.
mainPoints.explanation: A production-grade evaluation pipeline must include component evaluation, trajectory evaluation, task completion evaluation, and end-to-end business outcome evaluation, employing a hybrid evaluation strategy (unit tests, schema validation, rule engines, LLM-as-Judge, etc.).

mainPoints.point: Cost control is the lifeline of a production-grade agent, requiring real-time Token Budget scheduling.
mainPoints.explanation: Through model routing, context compression, and budget-based tiered degradation (green/yellow/red/circuit-breaker zones), a controllable balance between quality and cost can be achieved, while monitoring cost per unit of business outcome.

keyQuotes: Agents handle local intelligence, while the Harness handles global control.
A tool is not a function call; it is an authorization point for production resources.
Memory is not a warehouse; it is a garden. It needs regular pruning.
MCP makes tool integration cheap; the Harness makes tool invocation trustworthy.
Without a Harness, Multi-Agent is just a spectacle; with a Harness, agents can become productive.

relatedArticles.title: RAG is Dead? No, Grep is Back!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the leaked source code of Claude Code, this article deeply deconstructs its abandonment of RAG and vector retrieval in favor of an LLM-driven multi-round iterative Grep search mechanism. It compares this approach with Cursor and Codex, demonstrating the feasibility and design philosophy of a zero-index solution in code search scenarios.

relatedArticles.title: From Requirements to Deployment: A Comprehensive Leap in R&D Efficiency with Full AI Automation
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically explains how Tencent's audit team built a fully automated AI delivery platform to achieve end-to-end automation from requirements, design, development, testing to deployment, and shares its evolution path from L2 (human-machine collaboration) to L3 (full automation), along with core challenges, specific practices, and quantified benefits.

relatedArticles.title: You Don't Know Agent: Principles, Architecture and Engineering Practice - Tw93
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically sorts out the core engineering practices of Agent architecture, covering key technical dimensions such as Agent Loop, Harness, context engineering, tool design, memory systems, multi-Agent organization, evaluation and tracing, and demonstrates the implementation of design principles through the OpenClaw open-source implementation.

relatedArticles.title: Thinking About Agentic Engineering from First Principles
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically derives six core best practices for Agentic Engineering from first principles and introduces a modular, Skill-based open-source framework, aiming to combine engineering discipline with AI capabilities to reliably improve software engineering quality under complex constraints.

relatedArticles.title: What You Don't Know About Claude Code: Architecture, Governance, and Engineering Practices - Tw93
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of Claude Code's six-layer architecture and engineering practices, proposing a systematic Agent development methodology from context governance and skill design to a verification loop.

relatedArticles.title: Investing 10,000 RMB in AI: A Year of Tools, Practices, and Reflections
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A systematic summary of a veteran developer's practical experience in the AI wave, covering everything from MAC toolchain optimization and Harness Engineering architectural constraints to building an Agent-driven automated learning loop.

relatedArticles.title: From Context to Long-Term Memory: Architectural Design and Practice of LLM Memory Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically elaborates on the necessity of memory engineering for large language models and proposes a hierarchical management, active scheduling, and mind-map organization scheme based on the "Memory Operating System (MemOS)" architecture.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Hermes in One Article: How the New Top-Tier Agent Self-Evolves from Experience
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the core innovation of the Hermes Agent—the Skills closed-loop system—detailing its complete implementation mechanism, from experience extraction and knowledge storage to intelligent retrieval and self-improvement, along with its engineering trade-offs and security considerations.

relatedArticles.title: 5 Lessons Learned from 400 Million Tokens: What Happened When 6 AI Agents Wrote Code for 4 Days Straight?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through a four-day multi-agent automated programming experiment, this article reveals that 'glue code' and engineering stability are more challenging and critical than prompt design when building AI systems.
